entities.name: Assembly of First Nations
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Assembly of First Nations (AFN), the national advocacy organization representing the 634+ First Nations communities across Canada with an estimated 900,000+ people (status and non-status First Nations, Métis and Inuit represented by other bodies), is Canada's principal Indigenous political organization — the institutional voice through which First Nations exercise collective political advocacy on treaty rights, land claims, self-governance, resource development, and the ongoing implementation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's 94 Calls to Action.

The AFN emerged from the National Indian Brotherhood (NIB), which had itself emerged from the political mobilization triggered by Pierre Trudeau's 1969 White Paper — which proposed abolishing special Indigenous legal status and integrating First Nations as individual Canadian citizens, generating massive opposition that became the foundational moment of modern Indigenous political organizing in Canada. The NIB was reconstituted as the AFN in 1982, giving it a more democratic structure with elected regional chiefs.

The AFN has been central to landmark moments in Canadian Indigenous rights: opposing the 1969 White Paper, contributing to Section 35's constitutional recognition of Aboriginal rights in 1982, negotiating the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (2006), and responding to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's 2015 report. The discovery of unmarked graves at former residential school sites (2021) — where over 150,000 Indigenous children were forcibly removed from families — created a major national reckoning with which AFN worked closely. National Chief Phil Fontaine's public disclosure of residential school abuse (1990) was a pivotal moment in making this history visible.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Assembly of First Nations — opposing the 1969 White Paper, securing Section 35 constitutional rights, negotiating Canada's largest class action settlement for residential school survivors, and leading the national reckoning with unmarked graves — is the central institution in the ongoing reconciliation between Canada and First Nations peoples.
